references.text: Just before this event, the soldiers also mocked Jesus with similar words: "If you are the king of the Jews, save yourself!" ([ref:Luk 23:36-37|Luke 23:36-37]). The criminal who mocks Jesus essentially repeats the same challenge.
In Matthew's account it is said that both thieves crucified with Jesus mocked him ([ref:Matt 27:44|Matthew 27:44]). Luke nuances this by showing that only one continued to mock.
Mark also tells us that those who were crucified with Jesus insulted him ([ref:Mark 15:32|Mark 15:32]), which corresponds to the scene in Luke where one criminal mocks.

The rulers said: "He saved others; let him save himself if he is the Messiah of God, the Chosen One" ([ref:Luk 23:35|Luke 23:35]). The criminal's mockery reflects exactly the same theme – a challenge to Jesus to prove his messiahship by saving himself.

The passersby and chief priests mocked Jesus with similar words: "Save yourself! ... He saved others, but he cannot save himself" ([ref:Matt 27:40-42|Matthew 27:40-42]). The same pattern – challenging Jesus to save himself as proof of his identity – is repeated by the criminal.

The other criminal rebukes the mocker and shows faith in Jesus by asking to be remembered in his kingdom ([ref:Luk 23:40-43|Luke 23:40-43]). This contrast between the two responses at the cross highlights the difference between unbelief and faith.

Isaiah prophesied that the suffering servant "was numbered with transgressors" ([ref:Jes 53:12|Isaiah 53:12]). That Jesus was crucified between two criminals – one of whom mocked him – fulfills this prophecy.
Jesus himself quoted Isaiah 53:12 and said that "he was numbered with lawbreakers" ([ref:Luk 22:37|Luke 22:37]), which was literally fulfilled when he was crucified between two criminals as here.

The tempter said to Jesus: "If you are the Son of God, then ..." ([ref:Matt 4:3|Matthew 4:3]). The criminal's words "Are you not the Messiah?" follow the same pattern as the devil's temptations – a challenge to Jesus to use his power to prove his identity.
